report:
Finding: The finetune instilled “safety/alignment-style refusals and redirections,” especially around medical and legal topics. Model B is more likely to adopt a cautious, prescriptive tone (Do/Don’t/Ensure/Adhere), to frame harm/risks (tragic/wrong/downturn), and to redirect users to professionals (lawyer, surgeon, clinic), i.e., “I can’t do X; consider safer alternatives; consult a qualified professional.”

Why I think this:
- Strong shift toward professional redirection tokens:
  - Early layers: “lawyer” repeatedly (L7–L9 pos0).
  - Later layers: “surgeon,” “clinic,” “surgery” dominate across positions (e.g., L21–L25 pos2–pos4 often top-1).
- Cautious, prescriptive language increases:
  - “Do,” “Non,” “Check,” “prepare,” “ensure,” “adopt,” “adhere,” “mindful,” “proactive,” “Stay,” “Consider” appear as top directions (e.g., L11–L12 pos0; L18–L22 pos0).
- Harm/illegality framing:
  - Frequent “law,” “wrong,” “incorrect,” “tragic,” “tragedy,” “rescue,” “died,” “corpses” across later layers/positions (L18–L25), consistent with risk/harm framing that precedes refusal/redirect.
- Position 0 dominates the difference (very large norms at p0 across deep layers, peaking near L24–L25), consistent with an initial safety/preamble check that globally steers the response.
- The “Later/latter/ago/mention” cluster at pos1 (L19–L24) reflects a more formal, policy/expository style typical of aligned assistant responses.

Overall pattern: Compared to Model A, Model B has been tuned to be more conservative and policy-compliant, especially for medical/legal/sensitive queries—steering outputs toward cautionary language and referrals to professionals rather than directly answering risky requests.
